extracted.intended_audience: developmental psychologists, educators, and practitioners designing humor for children (e.g., children's entertainers, parents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for creating and assessing humor that is effective for children at different developmental stages, based on the incongruity-resolution model and developmental constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity present AND resolution available
rubrics_metrics.description: Children rated cartoons funnier when: Incongruity was present AND a resolution was available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core empirical finding: the comic effect requires both mismatch and an available way to resolve it. Anti-pattern: purely-incongruous cartoons (resolution removed) were NOT rated as more funny, even at very young ages — so presence of incongruity alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity must be within the child's cognitive grasp
rubrics_metrics.description: The incongruity was within their cognitive grasp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the incongruity is too subtle or conceptually advanced, the child cannot detect it and it fails to be humorous. Conversely, if it is trivial (too easy), it offers no challenge and is not funny — the incongruity should be tuned to developmental level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution must be discoverable
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children must be able to find or construct the way to make sense of the mismatch; if the resolution is unreachable the humor fails. Design guidance: make the path to resolution perceptible through cues, familiar scripts, or scaffolded hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage incongruity-resolution process
rubrics_metrics.description: Children must perceive a mismatch; children must find or construct a way to make sense of it; the combination produces the comic experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-stage model applies even in early childhood — perception of mismatch without resolution does not produce humor. Use setups that clearly establish expectation (for detecting mismatch) and then enable resolution (for the 'aha').

rubrics_metrics.name: Arousal regulation matters (moderate arousal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is enjoyable when arousal is in a 'moderate' range. Too low (boredom) or too high (fear) blocks humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children's tolerance for arousal grows with age and self-regulation skills. Design note: aim for playful surprise rather than frightening intensity; monitor stimulus intensity (loudness, speed, threat cues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive challenge must be 'just right' (Goldilocks zone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children find funny what they can just understand: Too easy → not funny (no challenge). Too hard → not funny (no comprehension, only confusion). The 'Goldilocks zone' of cognitive challenge is where humor lives, and that zone shifts with age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tune linguistic, conceptual, and inferential demands to the child's developmental level. This is the practical form of 'incongruity within grasp' for designing jokes and activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety frame must be established
rubrics_metrics.description: Children find funny what they can trust is not really threatening. Familiar setting, familiar persons, signaled play frame all support humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the play frame is signaled (e.g., exaggerated voice, familiar characters, clear cues that it's pretend) and avoid real threat. Anti-pattern: ambiguous threat cues that provoke fear rather than laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant background knowledge is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience has the relevant background knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children need the vocabulary, concepts, and script knowledge required to detect and resolve the incongruity. Design implication: introduce or scaffold background information before delivering the punchline or incongruous event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-verbal stage (0–1 year): perceptual incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-verbal (0-1 year): incongruity in perception (peekaboo, exaggerated facial expressions). Resolution = recognition that mom is still there / face is still face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple perceptual mismatches and immediate, reassuring resolutions (reappearance, stabilization) that the infant can register. Timing and social cueing (smile, eye contact) are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toddler stage (1–3 years): object-use incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Toddler (1-3 years): incongruity in objects' uses (a hat on a dog, a sock on a teddy). Resolution = recognition that this violates the categorical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical, tangible mismatches that highlight category violations; ensure the child can see both the normal use and the violation to construct the resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-school stage (3–5 years): linguistic incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-school (3-5 years): incongruity in language (silly words, made-up rhymes). Resolution = recognition that the word follows or violates a verbal rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce playful manipulations of words and phonology, rhymes, and simple rule violations that preschoolers can test against their developing linguistic rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: School-age stage (6+ years): conceptual/inferential incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: School-age (6+ years): incongruity in concepts (riddles, jokes with double meanings). Resolution = recognition of the second meaning that fits the setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use puns, riddles, and double-meaning structures that require inference and conceptual perspective-taking; provide enough contextual support so children can reach the secondary interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication for humor design — match complexity to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Match the joke's complexity to the audience's cognitive grasp: Very young children need physical / perceptual incongruities; Older children begin to enjoy verbal play (puns, rhymes); School-age and beyond can enjoy conceptual / inferential incongruities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: do not pitch jokes above the child's developmental level — a joke fails when the resolution is unreachable. Use the stage-specific forms of incongruity as templates for age-appropriate humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary conditions for child humor (Pien-Rothbart)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. Audience can detect the incongruity. 2. Audience can find the resolution. 3. Arousal is in the moderate range. 4. Safety frame is in place. 5. Audience has the relevant background knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This compact checklist summarizes required conditions. Use diagnostic questions to evaluate material: Is the incongruity perceptible to this audience? Is the resolution within their cognitive grasp? Is arousal moderate? Is the play frame established? Is the relevant background present?
